1	# Analog information preservation and gain policy {#sec-analog-preservation}
     2	
     3	A weak return can be absent from a digital record for two very different reasons:
     4	there was no return, or the analog path had not recovered enough to observe it.
     5	The second case cannot be repaired by lowering a detection threshold. The
     6	[feasibility and allocation treatment](feasibility-architecture-allocations.qmd)
     7	used supplied headroom and disturbance interfaces. Here we ask how an engineer
     8	could specify the stages and operating policy behind such an interface.
     9	
    10	The bounded task is a coherent radar receive path, with wanted power −100 dBm at
    11	1.000 GHz and two simultaneous blockers, each −20 dBm, at 1.010 and 1.020 GHz.
    12	All powers are delivered into matched 50 Ω planes. The desired output must exceed
    13	−60 dBm, the equivalent worst peak must remain below −10 dBm, and a steady
    14	in-band distortion phasor is allocated at most 0.02° phase displacement. After a
    15	known transmit exposure ends, usable weak-return data are required within 180 μs,
    16	with the incremental weak-signal transfer, relative to its unexposed same-state
    17	calibration, within 1 percent in magnitude and 0.1° in phase. The steady
    18	contamination and transient-response limits are separate subsystem criteria;
    19	neither is a total phase-measurement uncertainty requirement.
    20	These are illustrative requirements, not a radar specification or measured device
    21	behavior. They are a new multitone/pulse contrast, not a replacement for the
    22	single-blocker noise interfaces in Chapters 11–12.
    23	
    24	By the end of the argument, the reader should be able to allocate stage gain,
    25	noise and linearity; distinguish a low-level nonlinear approximation from a
    26	recovery model; execute a gain/valid-data policy; and identify the measurements
    27	needed before relying on that policy. Circuit synthesis and actual converter
    28	selection remain external or later refinements. A missing component guarantee
    29	will remain a conditional interface rather than a convenient numerical assumption.
    30	
    31	## Place prevention before the vulnerable stage {#sec-analog-stage-placement}
    32	
    33	Use four synthetic blocks: a selector with wanted loss 2 dB and blocker rejection
    34	$A_B$; an LNA with gain 20 dB and noise figure 2 dB; a conversion/IF block with
    35	gain 6 dB and noise figure 8 dB; and a backend with gain 20 dB and noise figure
    36	6 dB in its high state H. Noise figures describe linear, matched, 290 K small-signal
    37	conditions at the wanted frequency. Input third-order intercepts are respectively
    38	0, +20 and +25 dBm for the active blocks. Their qualified equivalent input peak
    39	ceilings are −15, −10 and −5 dBm. These ceilings delimit the intended linear/
    40	weakly nonlinear model; they are neither damage ratings nor inferred compression
    41	points. The readout ceiling is an additional interface.
    42	
    43	For state H, wanted gain from input P0 to output O is
    44	$-2+20+6+20=44$ dB, hence wanted power at O is −56 dBm. Selecting $A_B=49$ dB
    45	gives the following stage inputs:
    46	
    47	| Plane | Wanted, dBm | Each blocker, dBm | Worst composite peak, approximately dBm |
    48	|---|---:|---:|---:|
    49	| LNA input, after selector | −102 | −69 | −62.883 |
    50	| Conversion input | −82 | −49 | −42.883 |
    51	| Backend input | −76 | −43 | −36.883 |
    52	| Readout O | −56 | −23 | −16.883 |
    53	
    54	Equivalent peak power means $V_{\rm peak}^2/(2R)$, so that a single sinusoid has
    55	its ordinary delivered power. For coherent tones with arbitrary phases, add peak
    56	**voltages** before squaring. Writing powers in dBm, the conservative bound at O is
    57	
    58	$$
    59	P_{\rm pk}=20\log_{10}\!\left(2\,10^{P_B/20}+10^{P_S/20}\right)\ \mathrm{dBm}.
    60	$$ {#eq-analog-peak}
    61	
    62	The factors inside the logarithm are proportional to square roots of milliwatts;
    63	$P_B=26-A_B$ and $P_S=-56$ here. All phases can align at one instant, so the bound
    64	is attainable for the stated tones. With $A_B=49$, it gives −16.88271 dBm, or
    65	about 45.28 mV peak, comfortably below 100 mV. The weak tone belongs in the sum:
    66	even here its addition changes the two-blocker-only bound by 0.09669 dB. A modulated
    67	waveform requires a justified crest-factor bound over its actual support, not its
    68	average RMS alone. For $M$ equal tones, aligned peak power exceeds a single tone
    69	by $20\log_{10}M$, and exceeds their summed average power by $10\log_{10}M$.
    70	
    71	Moving the selector after the LNA preserves net wanted gain but exposes the LNA
    72	to −20 dBm per blocker: their aligned peak is about −13.979 dBm, above its −15 dBm
    73	qualification ceiling. The later filter cannot establish that the LNA remained
    74	linear. Nor does a backend attenuator protect that input.
    75	@fig-analog-prevention-paths makes the ordering and in-band generation explicit.
    76	
    77	![The early selector spends noise figure to protect the LNA; the same selector placed later cannot remove a product already generated at the wanted frequency. Stage values are synthetic interface requirements.](figures/analog-prevention-paths.svg){#fig-analog-prevention-paths fig-alt="Early and late selector arrangements have the same gain blocks. Early rejection reduces each blocker to minus69dBm at the LNA; late rejection leaves minus20dBm there. A third-order product coincides with the wanted1GHz frequency. Late selection has lower modeled noise figure but violates the LNA input envelope."}
    78	
    79	The noise cost follows by referring each stage's added noise to P0. If stage $i$
    80	has power gain $g_i$ and noise factor $F_i$, its added input-equivalent noise is
    81	$kT_0(F_i-1)$ W/Hz. The preceding power gains divide that contribution when
    82	referred farther upstream, giving
    83	
    84	$$
    85	F_{\rm total}=F_1+\frac{F_2-1}{g_1}
    86	 +\frac{F_3-1}{g_1g_2}+\cdots.
    87	$$
    88	
    89	A matched passive loss $L$ at $T_0$ has $g=1/L$ and $F=L$: the output remains at
    90	thermal equilibrium although the available wanted power falls. Substituting
    91	$L=10^{2/10}$ and the declared active stages gives **4.16292 dB** noise figure
    92	with early selection, versus **2.27054 dB** with selection immediately after the
    93	LNA. At a hypothetical 1 kHz rectangular noise bandwidth the early chain's
    94	input-equivalent thermal noise is −139.81227 dBm. That is only this analog linear
    95	model; it neither includes all later observation noise nor replaces Chapter 12's
    96	supplied complete floor. Correlated or mismatched noise requires Chapter 9's
    97	loaded source model rather than this scalar cascade.
    98	
    99	Isolation, drive and power are interfaces too. For an additive coherent aggressor
   100	of −20 dBm whose effective path ends at O, a 0.02° allocation with wanted −56 dBm
   101	requires its retained power below
   102	$-56+20\log_{10}(\sin0.02^\circ)\simeq-125.142$ dBm: at least 105.142 dB path
   103	loss from that aggressor plane, if it consumes the whole allocation. A component's
   104	reverse isolation alone is not that path; board, supply, enclosure and conversion
   105	paths can bypass it. Multiplicative supply-to-phase coupling instead needs its
   106	own sensitivity. Supplying 5 V at assumed currents 20, 30, 40 and 10 mA for the
   107	three active blocks and controls consumes 0.50 W/channel, before reference,
   108	converter and processing power. Three channels would spend 1.50 W of Chapter
   109	12's illustrative 2.4 W total envelope, leaving an **unproved** 0.90 W. Actual
   110	bias, LO drive/loading, impedance, thermal resistance and stage dissipation must
   111	be reconciled; this arithmetic selects no compatible component set.
   112	
   113	## Predict small distortion without extrapolating overload {#sec-analog-nonlinearity}
   114	
   115	For a real memoryless stage, begin with
   116	$y=a_1x+a_2x^2+a_3x^3$. Multiplying two cosine tones shows sum/difference and
   117	second-harmonic terms from $a_2$, and third-order components at $2f_1-f_2$ and
   118	$2f_2-f_1$. For equal peak input amplitudes $A$, the latter have amplitude
   119	$3|a_3|A^3/4$. The linear fundamental is $|a_1|A$. Their extrapolated equality
   120	defines $A_I^2=4|a_1|/(3|a_3|)$; with $P_I=A_I^2/(2R)$ this yields, in dBm,
   121	
   122	$$
   123	P_{{\rm IM3,in}}\simeq3P_{B,{\rm in}}-2\,\mathrm{IIP3}.
   124	$$ {#eq-analog-im3}
   125	
   126	This is the input-referred power of **one** product in the weak cubic region,
   127	not its actual measured value at arbitrary drive. Second-order products require
   128	analogous IP2 information and the full conversion/exclusion map in Chapter 11.
   129	[MT-012, Rev. A, pp. 2–4](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-012.pdf#page=2)
   130	explains the extrapolated RF intercept construction and why a generic intercept
   131	interpretation should not be transferred to converter clipping. Its plotted
   132	regimes do not certify our stages [@kesterMT012].
   133	
   134	Here $2(1.010)-1.020=1.000$ GHz: one IM3 product lands exactly on the wanted
   135	frequency. Refer each stage contribution through its remaining gain to O.
   136	For 49 dB rejection, the LNA, converter and backend generate output-equivalent
   137	products of **−161, −161 and −159 dBm**. Relative to −56 dBm wanted, their
   138	amplitude ratios add conservatively to
   139	
   140	$$
   141	r=10^{(-161+56)/20}+10^{(-161+56)/20}
   142	 +10^{(-159+56)/20}=1.83263\times10^{-5}.
   143	$$
   144	
   145	Unknown product phases require a phasor sum or its triangle bound, not an RSS of
   146	powers. The disk geometry from Chapter 12 gives phase displacement at most
   147	$\arcsin r=0.00105002^\circ$. Subsequent IM interactions and level-dependent
   148	transfer are neglected at this small-error order and need checking against the
   149	allocated margin. This result covers this product, not every spur or compression
   150	mechanism. @fig-analog-blocker-region compares it with the separate peak and
   151	operating-policy constraints.
   152	
   153	![Changing blocker rejection moves the composite peak, coherent product bound and gain-policy margins differently. The qualified readout ceiling, leaving high gain and returning to high gain are distinct boundaries.](figures/analog-blocker-region.svg){#fig-analog-blocker-region fig-alt="Composite wanted-plus-two-blocker peak decreases with selector rejection. It crosses minus10, minus13 and minus16dBm at different rejections. A second plot shows the cubic in-band phase bound falling below0.02degree. At49dB all illustrated inequalities pass; at46dB high gain cannot return after a low-state transition."}
   154	
   155	A band-centered complex envelope can represent narrowband AM-to-AM/PM behavior as
   156	$z_o=a z+b|z|^2z$. For the real cubic's selected band, $b=3a_3/4$; a complex $b$
   157	is a phenomenological envelope model of phase conversion, not a literal real
   158	instantaneous voltage polynomial. With $\eta=(b/a)|z|^2$, gain magnitude is
   159	$|a|\sqrt{(1+\Re\eta)^2+(\Im\eta)^2}$ and extra phase is
   160	$\operatorname{atan2}(\Im\eta,1+\Re\eta)$. These identities explain why amplitude
   161	calibration alone misses AM-to-PM. Fitting a complex coefficient requires complex
   162	response data at specified level, frequency and state.
   163	
   164	For example, write the selected input envelope as wanted amplitude $S$ and
   165	blocker amplitudes $B_1,B_2$ at offsets 10 and 20 MHz. In $|z|^2z$, products
   166	whose two positive offsets minus the conjugated offset equal zero contribute
   167	at the wanted frequency. Collecting them gives
   168	
   169	$$
   170	z_{o,0}=aS+b\left[S(|S|^2+2|B_1|^2+2|B_2|^2)+B_1^2B_2^*\right].
   171	$$
   172	
   173	The last term is additive contamination; the terms multiplying $S$ change the
   174	wanted transfer. For a weak wanted tone beside two strong blockers, that coefficient
   175	also contains $2(b/a)(|B_1|^2+|B_2|^2)$. In the pure cubic model,
